title: Little Women
author: Louisa May Alcott
level: Chinese junior-high (CEFR A2-B1). Simple English meanings.

impertinent.meaning: Rude to a person who should be treated with respect, such as a teacher.

prim.meaning: Too careful and proper in the way you look and act. Not easy and playful.

chit.meaning: A word for a girl or young woman, used when you think she is silly or too proud.

tomboy.meaning: A girl who likes boys' games and acts like a boy.

poky.meaning: Slow and not fun, with a small, poor life.

twilight.meaning: The soft, weak light in the evening after the sun has gone down.

recess.meaning: A place in a wall that goes back from the rest of the wall. Books can stand there.

pervaded.meaning: Spread through every part of a place.

chaplain.meaning: A church man who goes with an army to help the soldiers.

drafted.meaning: Chosen and ordered by the government to join the army.

incantation.meaning: Magic words that a person says or sings to make magic work.

slang.meaning: Rough, friendly words that people use in talk, but not in careful, proper speech.

crammed.meaning: Pushed in so full that nothing more could fit.

pious.meaning: Good in a quiet, religious way.

rummage.meaning: To search for something by moving things around.

vittles.meaning: Food. This is how Hannah says it.

huddled.meaning: Pressed close together in a small place to keep warm.

abashed.meaning: Feeling a little bad because people are looking at you.

impetuously.meaning: Very fast and without thinking, because of strong feeling.

gruel.meaning: A thin food made by cooking grain in water or milk. Sick people ate it.

trump.meaning: A kind person you can trust and like very much.

spangle.meaning: A small, flat, bright piece of metal put on clothes so that it catches the light.

doublet.meaning: A short, close coat that men wore long ago.

chintz.meaning: Cloth with a bright picture on it, used for window covers and chairs.

baize.meaning: Thick, soft green cloth, often used to cover tables.

philter.meaning: A magic drink that makes a person fall in love.

minion.meaning: A person who does what a strong person tells him to do.

serenade.meaning: A love song that a man sings outside the window of the woman he loves.

bequeaths.meaning: Gives away money or things to people after she has died.

garret.meaning: A small room at the top of a house, just under the top of the house.

comforter.meaning: A thick, warm cover for a bed. Here Jo puts it round herself.

poplin.meaning: A smooth cloth, used for everyday dresses.

mortified.meaning: Feeling very bad about yourself in front of other people.

caper.meaning: A fast, happy jump or run. 'Cut capers' means to jump and play around.

blithely.meaning: In a happy way, without worry.

tongs.meaning: A tool with two arms. Here it is made hot and used to make hair round and soft.

ringlet.meaning: A long, round piece of hair that goes round and round.

scorched.meaning: Hurt a little on the outside by too much heat.

snood.meaning: A soft net or band that a girl wears to hold her hair.

drab.meaning: A brown colour that is not bright.

rubber.meaning: A cover that goes over shoes to keep them dry in the rain.

blunderbuss.meaning: In a joke by Jo, a person who is not careful and breaks things.

skylarking.meaning: Playing and joking around instead of working.

forlornly.meaning: In a sad and lonely way.

trudge.meaning: To walk a long way slowly, with heavy steps, because you are tired.

midget.meaning: A very small person. Here Meg uses it in an angry way for the small children she teaches.

toil.meaning: To work very hard for a long time.

grumps.meaning: A bad, cross way of feeling. 'Had the grumps' means felt bad and cross.

turnover.meaning: A small hot food with a soft cover and something sweet inside.

bleak.meaning: Cold, empty and not nice, with nothing to keep you safe from the wind.

wretch.meaning: A person who is very sad or very bad. Here Jo uses it as a joke name.

infirm.meaning: Weak or not well. Here it is used for old, hurt things that a girl plays with and keeps.

repulsive.meaning: Very bad to look at; it makes you want to turn away.

caricature.meaning: A funny drawing that makes a person's face look strange, to make people laugh.

deportment.meaning: The way a person walks, stands and acts, especially in front of others.

reprimand.meaning: Angry words from a teacher or someone with power, for something you did wrong.

specs.meaning: Glasses that people wear on their eyes to see better.

betokening.meaning: Showing clearly that something is true; being a sign of it.

conservatory.meaning: A glass room, kept warm, where plants grow all year. It is part of a rich house.

listless.meaning: Tired and without interest or energy.

sallied.meaning: Went out quickly and bravely to do something.

pate.meaning: The head, or the top of the head. Here it is a funny word for Laurie's hair-covered head.

blancmange.meaning: A soft, sweet, white food made from milk. It is cold and smooth and is eaten with a spoon.

fidgety.meaning: Not able to keep still; always moving and worried.

elated.meaning: Very happy and proud because something good has happened.

redoubtable.meaning: Strong, and a little hard to face; a person you must respect.

evolutions.meaning: Planned movements. Here the boy makes funny movements to make a girl laugh.

glowered.meaning: Looked at someone with an angry, dark face.

gruff.meaning: Rough and low in voice or manner, but not truly unkind.

quaint.meaning: Old-fashioned in a pleasing, interesting way.

woo.meaning: To try to win the love of a person so that she will say yes to marriage.

benefactor.meaning: A person who gives money or help to others.

indolent.meaning: Not wanting to work; liking to do nothing.

truant.meaning: A child who stays away from school without leave. 'Play truant' means to do this.

coddling.meaning: Taking too much care of someone, as if he were weak or a baby.

nunnery.meaning: A house where religious women live together. Here it is a joke about the girls' house.

voraciously.meaning: In a very hungry way, wanting a very large amount.

enticement.meaning: Something nice that is offered to make a person do something.

anecdote.meaning: A short, interesting story about something that really happened.

crotchety.meaning: Easily made angry and hard to please, in a strange way.

gesticulating.meaning: Moving the hands and arms a lot to show something.

unseemly.meaning: Not right or proper for the place or person.

puckered.meaning: Pulled into small lines, like cloth that is pulled together.

crustiness.meaning: A rough and unfriendly way of speaking or acting.

countenance.meaning: The face, or the look on a person's face.

twitted.meaning: Made fun of someone about something, in an unkind way.

contraband.meaning: Not allowed by the rules or the law. Here the teacher uses it for a green fruit that is not allowed at school.

ferrule.meaning: To hit a child's hand with a flat piece of wood, as a school way to make the child sorry.

confiscated.meaning: Taken away from someone by a teacher or other person in power, because of a rule.

neuralgia.meaning: A sharp pain in the face or head.

exulted.meaning: Felt and showed great happiness, often because someone else has lost something.

inexorable.meaning: Not changed by anyone's feelings; hard and strong.

portentous.meaning: Giving a sign that something important or bad will come.

infringed.meaning: Broken. Here it is used for rules.

ignominious.meaning: Bringing great loss of respect, so that one feels bad.

benignant.meaning: Kind and gentle in the way a person looks or acts.

demoiselle.meaning: A young lady. It is the French word, used here as a joke for school girls.

bridled.meaning: Held the head high and showed anger because of something said.

fiddlesticks.meaning: A word that means 'what a silly thing to say!'

pacify.meaning: To make an angry person quiet and happy again.

breach.meaning: A break between people who were friends.

overtures.meaning: First steps made to be friends again after a fight.

plume.meaning: To feel proud of yourself and show it. 'Plume herself' means feel proud of herself.

crosspatch.meaning: A person who is often cross and in a bad way.

refractory.meaning: Hard to control; not doing what you want it to do.

blowzy.meaning: Red in the face, with hair that is not in good order.

dishevelled.meaning: Not in good order. It is used for hair or clothes.

dilapidated.meaning: Old, broken and in bad condition.

tarlatan.meaning: A thin, hard cloth, used for light party dresses.

sacque.meaning: A coat that a woman wore, not close to the body.

irksome.meaning: Making you feel tired and cross; hard and not interesting.

daunted.meaning: Made to feel afraid or less brave.

sumptuously.meaning: In a rich and costly way. Here it means eating very well.

repining.meaning: Feeling sad and saying so, because you do not have something.

dowdy.meaning: Not fashionable; looking old and not smart.

talisman.meaning: A small thing that people believe will keep them safe from bad things.

frizzled.meaning: Made into many tiny rings, as hair is.

alacrity.meaning: A quick, happy readiness to do something.

champagne.meaning: A French wine with bubbles, drunk at parties.

discreetly.meaning: In a careful way, so as not to cause trouble or share a secret.

unmaidenly.meaning: Not right for a young girl of that time.

plantation.meaning: A large place where one kind of plant is grown. Here Jo plans a big bed of tall yellow flower.

aspiring.meaning: Growing up high, as if it wants to reach something great.

mignonette.meaning: A garden plant with small, sweet flower.

larkspur.meaning: A tall garden plant with blue or white flower.

bower.meaning: A cool place in a garden, under plants that grow over a stick shape.

earwiggy.meaning: Full of small insects with sharp parts at the back.

portfolio.meaning: A flat case that holds papers. Here it is the name of the girls' club paper.

rite.meaning: A serious act done in a fixed way, such as at a church.

troubadour.meaning: A man who made love songs and played music long ago.

alcove.meaning: A small part of a room set back in the wall.

ruse.meaning: A clever plan to make people believe something that is not true.

prostrate.meaning: Lying flat on the ground, face down.

stratagem.meaning: A clever plan used to get something.

complacently.meaning: In a way that shows you are too pleased with yourself and think there will be no trouble.

grubbing.meaning: Working hard at jobs that are not fun. Here Jo uses it for hard work.

larder.meaning: A small room or box where food is kept.

saleratus.meaning: A white thing put in food so that it gets big and light when it is cooked.

palatable.meaning: Good to eat; nice in taste.

chagrin.meaning: A feeling of anger and being upset because you have failed.

spinster.meaning: A woman who is not married and is no longer young.

tartly.meaning: In a sharp, unkind way of speaking.

meagre.meaning: Too small in amount; not enough.

deaconed.meaning: Made to look better than it is, by putting the best fruit on the top. Here the fruit looks good but is not.

precipitately.meaning: Very fast, without thinking or waiting.

assuaged.meaning: Made less strong. Used for pain or sad feelings.

ennui.meaning: A tired feeling because you have nothing to do and are not interested. A French word.

furbish.meaning: To clean and make something old look new again.

nosegay.meaning: A small group of sweet flower.

gingham.meaning: Cloth with small squares on it.

commendation.meaning: Words that say that someone has done well.

atone.meaning: To do something to make up for a wrong.

remonstrated.meaning: Said that she did not agree and asked someone not to do something.

wherry.meaning: A light, small boat that people move with long sticks.

ubiquitous.meaning: Seeming to be in every place at the same time.

ruinous.meaning: Broken down and falling to pieces.

sepulchral.meaning: Deep, low and sad, like a voice from under the ground.

rigmarole.meaning: A long, silly story that goes on and on. Here it is the name of a game in which each person adds to a story.

lackadaisical.meaning: Showing a weak, dream-like way of acting, as if too tired or too sad to care.

patronizing.meaning: Acting kind but showing that you think you are better than the other person.

fastidious.meaning: Hard to please; careful about small things.

impromptu.meaning: Done without any plan or practice.

shirked.meaning: Avoided work that he should have done.

aromatic.meaning: Sweet to the nose, in a strong way.

hemlock.meaning: A kind of tree with soft green leaves that stay green all year, and with small, hard cases that hold its seed.

espied.meaning: Saw something, often something hard to see.

stints.meaning: Fixed amounts of work that a person has to finish.

delectable.meaning: Very nice. In the story it is the name the girls give their hill.

musingly.meaning: In a thoughtful way, as if dreaming.

steed.meaning: A horse, especially a fine one. An old, grand word.

brake.meaning: A thick group of tall plants. Here Meg holds a group of them in front of her face.

subjection.meaning: The state of being ruled and having to do what someone says.

pique.meaning: A short feeling of anger because someone has hurt your feelings.

receptacle.meaning: A container for keeping things in.

ordeal.meaning: A hard, painful experience that you must go through.

nettled.meaning: Slightly angry because of something that was said.

bandbox.meaning: A round box made of thin board, used to keep a woman's things for the head.

wheedler.meaning: A person who gets what he wants by saying sweet things he does not mean.

plummy.meaning: Very good and nice. Here Laurie uses it for an interesting piece of news.

jubilee.meaning: A time of great happiness and a party.

bedewed.meaning: Made wet with small drops. Here it means wet with water from the eyes.

billiard.meaning: A game played on a big table with balls and long sticks. In those days a billiard room was a place respectable girls thought bad.

treadmill.meaning: A big round thing that people or animals walk on and never get anywhere. Here it means days that never change.

heiress.meaning: A woman who will get a lot of money from a family member when that person dies.

spatted.meaning: Hit with the flat hand, quickly and many times.

panacea.meaning: Something that people believe will fix every trouble.

ninepence.meaning: A small amount of money; nine small pieces of old English money.

fervent.meaning: Very strong and honest in feeling.

solace.meaning: Help that you get when you are sad or in trouble.

prudent.meaning: Careful and sensible in what you do.

lamentation.meaning: Loud crying that shows great sadness.

bulletin.meaning: A short, official report that gives the latest news.

mandarin.meaning: A play man whose head moves up and down.

detains.meaning: Keeps someone in a place for longer than he wants.

forehanded.meaning: Careful to be ready in good time; thinking ahead.

didoes.meaning: Silly jokes and games. Here Hannah uses it for the way Laurie plays.

pewmonia.meaning: A wrong way of saying the name of a very bad sickness that makes it hard to take air in.

picket.meaning: A man who guards a camp at night. 'Picket duty' means this job.

praiseworthy.meaning: Good enough that people should say well done.

pendulum.meaning: The part that moves from side to side in a machine that tells the time, and keeps it going.

relapse.meaning: A return to a bad way after a time of getting better.

belladonna.meaning: A medicine made from a plant that can kill. At that time people took it to try to stop a bad sickness with red skin.

camphor.meaning: A white thing with a sharp, strong feel in the nose, used in medicine.

wheedlesome.meaning: Sweet and soft in speech, trying to get someone to agree.

stamina.meaning: The strength to keep going for a long time and stay healthy.

gallivanting.meaning: Going about for fun with no plan.

incoherent.meaning: Not clear and not making sense, because the person is ill or mixed up.

stupor.meaning: A heavy, sleep-like state in which a person cannot think or feel.

piteous.meaning: Very sad to see; making you feel sorry for someone.

parched.meaning: Very dry, because you are very hot or have not had a drink.

wan.meaning: Looking tired and not well, with a white face.

vigil.meaning: A time of staying up at night to watch over someone.

pallor.meaning: A very white face, from illness or fear.

hysterically.meaning: In a wild way that you cannot control, between laughing and crying.

electrified.meaning: Gave someone a sudden, strong surprise.

prosy.meaning: Long and not interesting, with nothing new in it.

docile.meaning: Quiet and easy to teach or control.

counteract.meaning: To work against something so as to stop its effect.

reprehensible.meaning: Bad enough that people say it is wrong.

hoarded.meaning: Kept and saved many things, often more than needed.

turban.meaning: A long cloth that is wrapped round the head.

brocade.meaning: Rich, heavy cloth with a raised picture in it, often with gold or silver.

rosary.meaning: A string of round pieces that some people use when they speak to God.

covet.meaning: To want something very much that is someone else's.

bequeath.meaning: To give your money or things to someone after you die.

codicil.meaning: A short note added to a will, to change it or add to it.

reposeful.meaning: Quiet and restful; full of peace.

miser.meaning: A person who loves money and keeps it all for himself, never spending it.

affable.meaning: Friendly and easy to talk to.

privations.meaning: The lack of things that you need, such as food, heat or nice things.

weathercock.meaning: A person who changes his mind or feelings very often. Mrs. March uses it for Laurie.

disconsolate.meaning: Very sad and with no one to help.

crisscross.meaning: In a wrong, mixed-up way, with lines going across each other.

incorrigible.meaning: Not able to be changed or made better, because of a bad way of acting.

retaliation.meaning: Something bad that you do to pay back someone who did something bad to you.

disapprobation.meaning: A strong feeling that something is wrong and bad.

cavalier.meaning: Not caring about what other people feel; rude and careless in the way of speaking.

insinuatingly.meaning: In a clever, soft way, not saying things straight, to get what you want.

propitiate.meaning: To make an angry person feel more friendly by doing something nice.

testiness.meaning: A quick, cross way of getting angry about small things.

penance.meaning: A hard thing you do to yourself to show that you are sorry.

abase.meaning: To make yourself seem low and small, to show you are sorry.

unquenchables.meaning: Here it is the name Jo and Laurie give themselves: people whose happy, playful plans cannot be stopped.

merino.meaning: A soft, fine cloth made from the hair of a farm animal with thick, soft hair.

afghan.meaning: A warm cover made from thick, soft hair of a farm animal, in many bright colors.

stampede.meaning: A sudden run of many people at once, with a lot of noise.

blemish.meaning: A small spot that makes something look worse.

reminisced.meaning: Talked about happy things from the past.

jungfrau.meaning: A word from another language for a young girl. Here it is the name for the cold white girl figure that Jo and Laurie made in the garden.

boon.meaning: Something good that you ask for; a great help.

philander.meaning: To play at love in a light, silly way. Here Jo says it is fun to watch other people do it.

coquetry.meaning: The way a girl acts so that a man likes her, but with no real love.

capricious.meaning: Changing suddenly, without a good reason.

peremptorily.meaning: In a way that allows no one to say no; as an order.

perversity.meaning: A wish to do what is not wanted of you.

dudgeon.meaning: A feeling of anger because someone has been rude to you. 'In high dudgeon' means very angry.

transfixed.meaning: Held still, because of great surprise or fear.

abject.meaning: Very low, with no good opinion of yourself.

delusion.meaning: A wrong idea that you hold strongly.

premise.meaning: To say something first, before the main part of the story.

bookkeeper.meaning: A person whose job is to write down in books the money a business gets and spends.

dandified.meaning: Too careful about clothes; dressing in a very fine way.

hazed.meaning: Played rough or unkind games on new students at college.

profusion.meaning: A very large amount of something.

expatiating.meaning: Talking for a long time about something.

degenerate.meaning: Becoming worse than in the past.

pinafore.meaning: A cover with no arms, worn over a dress to keep it clean.

damask.meaning: A fine, shiny cloth with a picture in it, used for table covers.

whatnot.meaning: A light stand with open places, one over the other, for small things.

loath.meaning: Not willing; not wanting to do something.

indecorous.meaning: Not polite or proper for the time and place.

moire.meaning: A fine cloth with a look like water moving.

salver.meaning: A flat metal thing for carrying glasses or food.

nectar.meaning: In old stories, the sweet drink of the gods. Here it is a joke word for the drinks at the wedding.

quakeress.meaning: A woman of the Quaker religion, who wore simple, soft-colored clothes.

tribute.meaning: Something given to show love, thanks or respect.

cravat.meaning: A cloth that a man wears round his neck.

wrought.meaning: Made or brought about. Here it is used for the changes that time has made.

audacity.meaning: A brave, rude way of acting that does not fear what others think.

promiscuously.meaning: Here and there, without order or care.

ardor.meaning: Strong, warm feeling, or great wish to do something.

lurid.meaning: Very bright in a strange, bad way.

ogress.meaning: A woman in old stories who is a bad, giant monster.

suavity.meaning: A smooth and polite way of acting.

foible.meaning: A small weakness or silly way of acting in a person's character.

surfeit.meaning: Too much of something, especially food.

vortex.meaning: A fast turn, like water going round and round. Here Jo uses it for a time when she writes and writes.

afflatus.meaning: A strong flow of ideas that seems to come from a higher power.

rakishly.meaning: In a careless, brave way, a little to one side.

matrons.meaning: Older married women, who look serious and proper.

tatting.meaning: A kind of fine cloth with holes in it, made by hand.

bandana.meaning: A large cloth, often red or yellow, that people wear on the head or round the neck.

labyrinth.meaning: A place with so many ways that it is easy to get lost.

denouement.meaning: The end of a story, where all is made clear.

elopement.meaning: Running away secretly to get married.

digress.meaning: To move away from the main subject while talking or writing.

perusal.meaning: The act of reading something with care.

ruthlessly.meaning: With no feeling for the pain of others.

dyspeptic.meaning: Having a bad stomach because of food that is too rich.

bounteous.meaning: Very kind in giving; more than enough.

frugal.meaning: Careful not to spend much money.

pungent.meaning: Having a strong, sharp taste or nose feeling.

derisive.meaning: Showing that you think someone is silly; laughing at them.

furbelows.meaning: Extra pieces of cloth on a dress, for show.

countermanded.meaning: Said no to an order that was given before.

gingerly.meaning: In a very careful way, as if afraid of breaking something.

greatcoat.meaning: A long, heavy coat worn in cold weather.

phlegm.meaning: A quiet way of acting that does not get excited.

conducive.meaning: Helping to bring about a certain result.

assuage.meaning: To make a pain or bad feeling less strong.

bemoan.meaning: To show sadness about something with loud, sorry words.

mantua.meaning: A woman's dress that is not close to the body. A 'mantua-maker' makes dresses.

organdie.meaning: A very thin, hard cloth, used for summer dresses.

demure.meaning: Quiet and serious in a polite way, often to look good.

blandly.meaning: In a smooth way that shows no feeling.

volubly.meaning: In a way that talks a lot and very fast.

effusion.meaning: A showing of feeling that is too strong and goes on too long.

connoisseur.meaning: A person who knows a lot about art or fine things and can judge them well.

puritanical.meaning: Too hard about what is right and wrong, and against fun.

brusque.meaning: Quick and rude in speaking, with no polite words.

parasol.meaning: A light cover that a woman holds up to keep the sun off her.

irreproachable.meaning: Perfect; with nothing that anyone can find wrong.

akimbo.meaning: With hands on the sides of the body and the arms pointing out.

eclipsed.meaning: Was so good that it made another thing look less good.

rankled.meaning: Kept causing a bitter, angry feeling for a long time.

expediency.meaning: Doing what is useful for a plan, even if it is not fair.

disconsolately.meaning: In a very sad way that no one can change.

vellum.meaning: A fine kind of paper made from animal skin, used for special books.

illuminated.meaning: Drawn with bright colors and gold, like the big letters in old books.

conciliatory.meaning: Meant to stop a fight and make peace.

phalanx.meaning: A close group of people moving together, like soldiers.

repinings.meaning: Sad words about not having something.

magnanimous.meaning: Very kind and good, especially to an enemy.

uncharitableness.meaning: Being unkind in thought about other people.

hansom.meaning: A light coach, pulled by one horse, that anyone can pay to ride in. It moves on two big round parts, and the driver sits up behind.

barouche.meaning: A fine open coach, pulled by horses, with a top that can be pushed back.

postilions.meaning: Men who ride one of the horses that pull a coach, to guide them.

dowagers.meaning: Old ladies of high position, often women whose husbands have died.

colliery.meaning: A place where men get black fuel from under the ground.

gallows.meaning: A wood structure on which bad people were killed with a rope.

bootblack.meaning: A person, often a boy, who cleans people's shoes for money.

latticed.meaning: Having crossed pieces of wood or metal, as in an old window.

mortifies.meaning: Makes someone feel very bad about themselves.

biddies.meaning: Birds that give eggs. The word can also mean old women who talk a lot.

woodbine.meaning: A plant that goes up walls, with sweet flower.

evaded.meaning: Got away from a question without a direct answer.

disquietude.meaning: A feeling of worry and not being at peace.

reverie.meaning: A state of thinking about nice things, like a dream.

pummelled.meaning: Hit again and again with the hands or something hard.

coxcomb.meaning: A silly young man who is too proud of his looks and clothes.

eligible.meaning: Good enough to be chosen, especially as a husband, because of money or position.

admonitory.meaning: Giving a warning or a gentle telling-off.

acquiesced.meaning: Agreed to something without saying no.

assiduity.meaning: Great care and attention that does not stop.

patriarch.meaning: A very old and respected man who is the head of a family.

horsehair.meaning: Hair from a horse, used in chairs.

insinuating.meaning: Trying in a clever, soft way to make someone like you.

slipshod.meaning: Careless and not in good order, as in speech.

gabble.meaning: Fast talk that is hard to understand.

rummaging.meaning: Searching for something by turning things over.

meerschaum.meaning: A soft, white stone. Here it means a thing for smoking made from this stone.

hyacinth.meaning: A spring flower, sweet to the nose, that grows from a round thing under the ground.

standish.meaning: A stand that holds the things used for writing on a table.

brocades.meaning: Rich, heavy cloth with a raised picture in it, often with gold or silver.

whippersnappers.meaning: Young people who think they are important, but are not.

effervescence.meaning: Lively, happy feeling that bubbles up.

roughshod.meaning: In a hard way, with no care for others' feelings. 'Ride roughshod over' someone means to treat him badly.

boggled.meaning: Done badly, so that it is out of shape.

kobolds.meaning: In German stories, small spirits who live in houses or under the ground.

bashful.meaning: Not comfortable with people; easily upset in front of them.

concocted.meaning: Made up a story or plan by putting ideas together.

discomfiture.meaning: A feeling of being upset and mixed up when things go wrong.

banditti.meaning: Bad men who live in the hills and take things from people on the road.

emaciated.meaning: Very thin because of too little food. Here it is a joke about a bag with no money in it.

harrowing.meaning: Causing great fear or pain in the mind.

didactic.meaning: Meant to teach, especially about right and wrong.

lucre.meaning: Money, as something low. It is a joke name for money.

inconsolable.meaning: So sad that no one can make them feel better.

levee.meaning: A party where many people come to meet an important person.

inflammable.meaning: Easy to set on fire. Here it means very easy to move to strong feeling.

cumbrous.meaning: Heavy and hard to move in.

threshold.meaning: The bottom part of a door, where you step in.

novice.meaning: A person who is new to a job and has little experience.

allayed.meaning: Made a fear or worry less strong.

stile.meaning: Steps over a wall, so that people can cross but animals cannot.

impetuosity.meaning: Acting fast and with strong feeling, without thinking first.

decapitated.meaning: Cut off the head of something.

penitent.meaning: Feeling sorry for having done wrong.

marplot.meaning: A person who gets in the way and makes a plan go wrong.

paragraphs.context: Do you remember how you used to play 'Pilgrim's Progress' when you were little things
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. March reminds the girls of their old game of Pilgrim's Progress. They played it all through the house.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. March ended the quiet after Jo's words. In her cheerful voice she asked the girls if they remembered playing 'Pilgrim's Progress' when they were small. She said nothing made them happier than when she tied her piece-bags on their backs as heavy loads. She gave them hats, sticks and rolls of paper, and let them travel through the house. They began in the cellar, the City of Destruction, and went up and up to the housetop. There they put all the lovely things they could find, to make a Celestial City.

paragraphs.context: Very clever were some of their productions
paragraphs.mainIdea: The girls were not rich, so they made their own things for the play. Some of them were very clever.
paragraphs.simple: The kind acts and ceremonies of the morning took so much time that the rest of the day was used to get ready for the evening party. The girls were still too young to go to the theatre often, and not rich enough to pay much for plays at home. So they used their wits. Need is the mother of invention, and they made everything they needed. Some of their work was very clever: guitars made of pasteboard, old lamps made from old-style butter-boats covered with silver paper, rich robes of old cotton shining with tin spangles from a pickle factory, and armor covered with the same useful diamond-shaped pieces. These were left in sheets when the lids of tin preserve-pots were cut out. The furniture was used to being turned upside down, and the big bedroom was the place of many innocent games.

paragraphs.context: After various lesser mishaps, Meg was finished at last
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sisters are ready for the party in their simple clothes. Their shoes and pins hurt, but they want to look elegant.
paragraphs.simple: After some smaller troubles, Meg was ready at last. With the whole family helping, Jo's hair was put up and her dress put on. They looked very good in their plain clothes. Meg wore a dull silver-gray dress with a blue velvet snood, lace frills and the pearl pin. Jo wore dark red-brown with a stiff, boyish linen collar and one or two white chrysanthemums as her only ornament. Each girl put on one nice light glove and carried one dirty glove, and all said it looked 'quite easy and fine'. Meg's high-heeled slippers were very tight and hurt her, but she would not say so. Jo's nineteen hairpins all seemed to be stuck straight into her head, which was not very comfortable. But dear me, they said, they would be elegant or die!

paragraphs.context: When Mr. March lost his property in trying to help an unfortunate friend
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. March lost his money, so Meg took a job as a governess. She finds being poor hard because she remembers better days and sees rich girls' pleasures.
paragraphs.simple: When Mr. March lost his money trying to help a friend in trouble, the two oldest girls asked to be allowed to do something to support themselves, at least. Their parents thought the girls could not start too early to build up energy, hard work and independence. So they agreed, and both girls began work with a hearty good will which, in spite of all troubles, is sure to win in the end. Margaret found a job as a nursery governess and felt rich with her small pay. As she said, she was 'fond of luxury', and her main trouble was being poor. She found this harder to bear than the others did, because she remembered a time when home was beautiful, life was full of ease and pleasure, and nobody needed anything. She tried not to be jealous or unhappy, but it was natural for a young girl to long for pretty things, happy friends, skills like music, and a happy life. At the Kings' house she saw every day all that she wanted. The older sisters of the children had just come out into society. Meg often saw pretty ball-dresses and bouquets, heard lively talk about theatres, concerts, sleigh parties and fun of every kind, and saw money spent freely on small things which would have meant so much to her. Poor Meg seldom complained, but a feeling that life was unfair sometimes made her bitter toward everyone. She had not yet learned how rich she was in the blessings which alone can make life happy.

paragraphs.context: Meg went back to toast her feet and read Ivanhoe
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo digs paths in the snow. The garden is between the Marches' shabby old house and the rich, lonely Laurence house.
paragraphs.simple: Meg went back to warm her feet and read Ivanhoe, and Jo began to dig paths with great energy. The snow was light, and with her broom she soon swept a path all round the garden, for Beth to walk in when the sun came out. The sick dolls needed air. The garden was between the Marches' house and Mr. Laurence's house. Both stood at the edge of the city, which still looked like the country, with small woods, lawns, large gardens and quiet streets. A low hedge divided the two properties. On one side was an old brown house that looked rather bare and shabby, because the vines that covered its walls in summer, and the flowers around it, were gone. On the other side was a fine stone house that clearly showed every kind of comfort and wealth, from the big coach-house and well-kept grounds to the greenhouse and the lovely things people could see between the rich curtains. But it seemed a lonely house with no life in it. No children played on the lawn, no mother's face smiled at the windows, and few people went in or out, except the old gentleman and his grandson.

paragraphs.context: But Beth, though yearning for the grand piano, could not pluck up courage
paragraphs.mainIdea: Beth is too afraid to go to the Laurence house, so Mr. Laurence finds a clever way to help her.
paragraphs.simple: Beth wanted the grand piano very much, but she could not find the courage to go to the 'Mansion of Bliss', as Meg called it. She went once with Jo. But the old gentleman did not know that she was shy. He stared hard at her from under his heavy eyebrows and said 'Hey!' so loudly that she was very afraid. She told her mother that her feet 'chattered on the floor'. She ran away and said she would never go there again, not even for the dear piano. Nothing anyone said or offered could take away her fear. Then Mr. Laurence heard about it in some mysterious way, and he began to put things right. During one of his short visits, he cleverly turned the talk to music. He talked about great singers he had seen and fine organs he had heard, and he told such charming stories that Beth could not stay in her far corner. She came nearer and nearer, as if under a spell. She stopped at the back of his chair and stood listening, with her great eyes wide open and her cheeks red with the excitement. Mr. Laurence paid her no more attention than if she had been a fly. He went on talking about Laurie's lessons and teachers. Then, as if the idea had just come to him, he spoke to Mrs. March.

paragraphs.context: too proud to cry or beseech, Amy set her teeth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Davis hits Amy's hand. The blows are not hard, but she feels deep shame because it is the first time.
paragraphs.simple: 'Your hand, Miss March!' was the only answer to her silent begging. Amy was too proud to cry or to beg. She pressed her teeth together, threw back her head, and took several stinging blows on her small hand without pulling away. The blows were not many or hard, but that did not matter to her. It was the first time in her life that anyone had hit her. To her, the shame was as deep as if he had knocked her to the ground.

paragraphs.context: The patience and the humility of the face she loved so well
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo learns from her mother's example. Knowing her mother has the same fault helps her to want to change.
paragraphs.simple: The patience and gentle, humble look on the face she loved so much taught Jo more than the wisest talk or the hardest words of blame. She felt comfort at once from her mother's kindness and trust in her. Knowing that her mother had a fault like hers, and tried to fix it, made her own fault easier to bear. It also made her more sure that she would cure it. But forty years seemed a long time to watch and pray, to a girl of fifteen.

paragraphs.context: The Moffats were very fashionable, and simple Meg was rather daunted
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meg enjoys the rich life at the Moffats' house and begins to copy them. She then feels poor and unhappy about her home.
paragraphs.simple: The Moffats were very fashionable, and Meg, who liked simple things, was a little afraid at first because the house was so grand and the people so elegant. But they were kind people in spite of their light, silly way of life, and soon made their guest feel at ease. Perhaps Meg felt, without knowing why, that they were not very educated or clever, and that all their show could not quite hide what they were really made of. It was certainly pleasant to eat rich food, ride in a fine carriage, wear her best dress every day and do nothing but enjoy herself. It suited her well, and soon she began to copy the manners and talk of the people around her. She put on small airs, used French words, curled her hair, made her dresses smaller and talked about fashion as well as she could. The more she saw of Annie Moffat's pretty things, the more she was jealous of her and wished to be rich. Now home looked bare and sad when she thought of it, and work seemed harder than ever. She felt she was a very poor girl who was badly treated, in spite of her new gloves and silk stockings.

paragraphs.context: As spring came on, a new set of amusements became the fashion
paragraphs.mainIdea: In spring the sisters work in the garden. Each has her own plot, and each plot shows the girl's character.
paragraphs.simple: When spring came, a new set of games became fashionable, and the longer days gave long afternoons for work and play. The garden had to be put in order, and each sister had one quarter of the small piece of land to do what she liked with. Hannah used to say that she would know which garden belonged to which girl, even if she saw them in China. She was right, because the girls' tastes were as different as their characters. Meg's garden had roses, heliotrope, myrtle and a small orange-tree. Jo's bed was never the same from one season to the next, because she always tried new things. This year it was to be a big bed of sunflowers, whose seeds were to feed 'Aunt Cockle-top' and her chicks. Beth grew old-style, sweet-smelling flowers, such as sweet peas, mignonette, larkspur, pinks, pansies and southernwood, with chickweed for the bird and catnip for the cats. Amy had a shady corner in hers. It was small and full of earwigs, but very pretty, with honeysuckles and morning-glories hanging their colored flowers over it, tall white lilies, soft ferns and as many bright, pretty plants as would agree to grow there.

paragraphs.context: The unusual spectacle of her busy mother rocking comfortably
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo is amazed to see her always-busy mother resting and reading in the morning.
paragraphs.simple: Jo was not used to seeing her busy mother rocking in a chair and reading so early in the morning. It made Jo feel that something unnatural had happened. An eclipse, an earthquake or a volcano would hardly have seemed stranger to her.

paragraphs.context: Oh, yes; of course it's very nice and proper in them to do so
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Kate talks as if Meg's work as a governess is a little shameful. Her proud tone hurts Meg's feelings.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Kate said that of course it was very nice and right for the American girls to work. She said that many fine, respectable young women in her country did the same and worked for noble families. They were the daughters of gentlemen, so they were well brought up and had many skills. Miss Kate spoke in a proud, 'I am better than you' way. This hurt Meg's pride and made her work seem not only less pleasant but also low and shameful to her.

paragraphs.context: Laurie lay luxuriously swinging to and fro in his hammock
paragraphs.mainIdea: Laurie is in a bad mood after a lazy, unhappy day. He sees the Marches go out and wonders what they are doing.
paragraphs.simple: On a warm September afternoon, Laurie lay in his hammock, swinging gently. He wondered what his neighbors were doing, but was too lazy to go and find out. He was in one of his moods. The day had brought him nothing good, and he wished he could live it again. The hot weather made him lazy. He had avoided his studies and tested Mr. Brooke's patience to the limit. He had made his grandfather angry by playing the piano for half the afternoon. He had scared the maids almost out of their minds by saying for fun that one of his dogs was going mad. After an angry talk with the stableman about a horse he thought was not cared for, he had thrown himself into the hammock. He was angry at the stupidity of the world until the peace of the lovely day made him calm in spite of himself. He looked up into the dark green of the horse-chestnut trees and dreamed many dreams. He was just imagining himself on the sea, on a trip round the world, when voices brought him back at once. He looked through the net of the hammock and saw the Marches coming out, as if they were going on a journey.

paragraphs.context: If anyone had been watching her, he would have thought her movements decidedly peculiar
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo goes to a newspaper office in town but is too nervous to go in. She walks up and down in the street, and Laurie watches her.
paragraphs.simple: If anyone had watched Jo, he would have thought her actions very strange. When she got off the bus, she walked very fast to a certain number in a certain busy street. She found the place with some trouble, went to the door and looked up the dirty stairs. After standing completely still for a minute, she suddenly ran back into the street and walked away as fast as she had come. She did this several times, and it greatly amused a black-eyed young man who was resting in a window of the building across the street. When she came back for the third time, Jo gave herself a shake, pulled her hat over her eyes and went up the stairs, looking as if she were going to have all her teeth pulled out.

paragraphs.context: Everyone scattered like leaves before a gust of wind
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. March is overwhelmed by the many jobs, and the girls work for her. The happy home is suddenly broken up.
paragraphs.simple: Writing, thinking and giving orders all at once might well confuse the poor lady. Meg begged her to sit quietly in her room for a little while and let the girls work. Everyone ran off in different ways, like leaves in front of a strong wind. The quiet, happy house was broken up as suddenly as if the paper had been an evil spell.

paragraphs.context: In the cold gray dawn the sisters lit their lamp
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sisters decide to be brave and not cry when their mother leaves. It is hard, because the house feels strange and their mother looks tired.
paragraphs.simple: In the cold gray early morning the sisters lit their lamp and read their chapter very seriously. A real trouble had come, so the little books were full of help and comfort. As they dressed, they agreed to say goodbye with hope and cheer, and not to make their mother sad with tears or complaints on her worried journey. Everything seemed strange when they went down. It was dim and still outside, but full of light and noise inside. Breakfast so early seemed odd, and even Hannah's face looked strange as she hurried round the kitchen in her nightcap. The big trunk stood ready in the hall, and mother's cloak and bonnet lay on the sofa. Mother sat trying to eat, but she was so pale and tired from lack of sleep and worry that the girls found it very hard to keep their plan. Meg's eyes kept filling with tears. Jo had to hide her face in the kitchen roller more than once. The two little girls looked serious and troubled, as if sorrow were new to them.

paragraphs.context: All were unconscious that this experience was a test of character
paragraphs.mainIdea: The girls think they did well and deserve praise. They then stop trying hard, and this leads to trouble.
paragraphs.simple: None of the girls knew that this time was a test of their character. When the first excitement was over, they thought they had done well and deserved praise. They did, but their mistake was to stop doing well. They learned this lesson through much worry and sorrow.

paragraphs.context: Hannah, quite worn out, lay down on the sofa at the bed's foot
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hannah sleeps, Mr. Laurence walks up and down, and Laurie lies by the fire. They all wait for Mrs. March to arrive.
paragraphs.simple: Hannah was very tired. She lay down on the sofa at the foot of the bed and fell fast asleep. Mr. Laurence walked up and down in the parlor. He felt that he would rather face an enemy gun than Mrs. March's worried face when she came in. Laurie lay on the rug and pretended to rest, but he looked into the fire with the thoughtful look that made his black eyes soft and clear.

paragraphs.context: If it had not been for Laurie, and old Esther, the maid
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy finds life at Aunt March's hard. The parrot and the dog are bad, and only Laurie and Esther make it bearable.
paragraphs.simple: Without Laurie and old Esther, the maid, Amy felt she could never have got through that terrible time. The parrot alone was enough to drive her mad. He soon felt that she did not admire him, and he took revenge by being as naughty as he could. He pulled her hair whenever she came near him. He upset his bread and milk to annoy her just after she had cleaned his cage. He made Mop bark by pecking at him while Madam slept. He called her names in front of visitors, and in every way acted like a bad old bird. She could not stand the dog either. He was a fat, cross animal who snarled and barked at her when she washed and brushed him. When he wanted food, which was about twelve times a day, he lay on his back with his legs in the air and a very silly look on his face. The cook was bad-tempered, the old coachman was deaf, and Esther was the only one who ever paid any attention to the young lady.

paragraphs.context: Money is a good and useful thing, Jo; and I hope my girls
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. March says money is useful, but she does not want a rich husband for Meg. She believes a good man's heart is worth more than a fortune.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. March said money is a good and useful thing and she hoped her girls would never need it too badly or be tempted by too much of it. She wanted John to have a good business with enough pay to stay out of debt and keep Meg comfortable. She did not want a great fortune, a high place in society or a famous name for her girls. If high rank and money came with love and goodness, she would gladly accept them. But she knew from her own life how much true happiness a plain little house could hold, where the daily bread is earned and having less makes the few pleasures sweeter. She was content to see Meg begin humbly, because she would be rich in having a good man's heart, and that was better than a fortune.

paragraphs.context: Jo's face was a study next day, for the secret rather weighed upon her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo is keeping a secret and finds it hard. Meg does not ask, so Jo acts proud, and Meg is annoyed. Jo fears Laurie will get the secret from her.
paragraphs.simple: Next day Jo's face was a sight to see, because the secret was a heavy weight on her and she found it hard not to look mysterious and important. Meg saw this but did not ask questions. She had learned that the best way to deal with Jo was to do the opposite of what Jo expected, so she felt sure that Jo would tell everything if she did not ask. She was surprised that Jo stayed silent, and that Jo acted in a superior way. This made Meg very annoyed, and she became cold and stiff and spent her time with her mother. This left Jo alone, because Mrs. March had taken her place as nurse and told her to rest, take exercise and enjoy herself after her long time indoors. With Amy gone, Laurie was Jo's only refuge. She enjoyed his company, but she rather feared him just then, because he was a tease who could not be stopped, and she was afraid he would coax her secret out of her.

paragraphs.context: Several days of unusually mild weather fitly ushered in a splendid Christmas Day
paragraphs.mainIdea: Christmas Day is wonderful. Jo and Laurie have made a surprise for Beth: a snow-girl in the garden with gifts.
paragraphs.simple: Several days of very mild weather were a fitting start to a fine Christmas Day. Hannah felt in her bones that it would be a very fine day, and she was right, because everyone and everything seemed sure to bring great success. First, Mr. March wrote that he would soon be with them. Then Beth felt unusually well that morning. She was dressed in her mother's gift, a soft red wool wrapper, and was carried like a queen to the window to see the gift from Jo and Laurie. The Unquenchables had done their best to deserve their name. Like elves they had worked at night, and had made a funny surprise. In the garden stood a grand snow-girl with holly on her head. In one hand she held a basket of fruit and flowers, and in the other a big roll of new music. Round her cold shoulders was a wool cover as bright as a rainbow, and a Christmas song came from her lips on a pink paper streamer.

paragraphs.context: Now Aunt March possessed in perfection the art of rousing the spirit of opposition
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aunt March's order not to like John makes Meg decide that she will. When we are young and in love, we like to do the opposite of what we are told.
paragraphs.simple: Aunt March was perfect at making even the gentlest people want to oppose her, and she enjoyed it. The best of us have a little wish to do the opposite, especially when we are young and in love. If Aunt March had begged Meg to accept John Brooke, Meg would probably have said she could not think of it. But because she was ordered not to like him, she at once decided that she would. Her own wish as well as this stubborn feeling made the decision easy. She was already very excited, so she opposed the old lady with unusual spirit.

paragraphs.context: The three years that have passed have brought but few changes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Three years have passed and the war is over. Mr. March is at home, working quietly as a minister and a scholar.
paragraphs.simple: In the three years that have passed, the quiet family has changed very little. The war is over and Mr. March is safe at home, busy with his books and his small church. In him the church found a minister both by nature and by calling. He was a quiet man who liked to study and was rich in a wisdom that is better than learning. He had a kindness that calls all people 'brother', and a goodness that grows into a fine character.

paragraphs.context: There were to be no ceremonious performances, everything was to be as natural
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wedding is simple and homelike. Aunt March is shocked to see the bride, the groom and the minister doing everyday things.
paragraphs.simple: There were to be no formal shows. Everything was to be as natural and homelike as possible. So when Aunt March arrived, she was shocked. The bride came running to welcome her and lead her in. The bridegroom was putting up a garland that had fallen down. She also saw the minister, the bride's father, marching upstairs with a serious face and a wine-bottle under each arm.

paragraphs.context: If “genius is eternal patience,” as Michelangelo affirms, Amy certainly had some claim
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy never gave up her art in spite of failures. She believed she would one day make real 'high art'.
paragraphs.simple: Michelangelo says that genius is patience that never ends. If that is true, Amy had some right to be called a genius, because she went on in spite of all troubles, failures and discouragement. She firmly believed that in time she would make something worth calling 'high art'.

paragraphs.context: Her “scribbling suit” consisted of a black woollen pinafore on which she could wipe her pen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo wears a special writing cap. Its position tells her family how her work is going.
paragraphs.simple: Jo's 'scribbling suit' was a black wool pinafore, on which she could wipe her pen as she liked, and a cap of the same cloth with a cheerful red bow. She stuffed her hair into the cap when she was ready for hard work. The family saw the cap as a signal and kept away during these times. They only put their heads in now and then to ask, 'Does genius burn, Jo?' They did not always dare even to ask, but looked at the cap and judged. If it was pulled low on her forehead, hard work was going on. In exciting moments it was pushed to one side. When she felt despair, it was pulled off and thrown on the floor. Then anyone who came in quietly went away, and no one dared speak to Jo until the red bow stood up happily on her head again.

paragraphs.context: Fired with a housewifely wish to see her storeroom stocked with homemade preserves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meg tries to make currant jelly like Hannah. She works all day, but the jelly will not set.
paragraphs.simple: Meg wished very much to see her storeroom full of jelly and fruit she had made herself. So she decided to make her own currant jelly. John was asked to send home a dozen little pots and extra sugar, because their own currants were ripe and had to be dealt with at once. John firmly believed his wife could do anything, and he was proud of her skill. He wanted her to be pleased and to save their only crop of fruit for winter. Home came four dozen little pots, half a barrel of sugar, and a small boy to pick the currants. Meg tucked her hair into a cap, bared her arms to the elbow, and put on a checked apron. She began work sure of success, because she had seen Hannah do it hundreds of times. The many pots surprised her, but John loved jelly and the jars would look nice on the top shelf, so she decided to fill them all. She spent a long day picking, boiling, straining and fussing. She did her best, asked Mrs. Cornelius for advice, and tried to remember what Hannah did. She boiled and sugared it again, but that dreadful stuff would not 'jell'.

paragraphs.context: Jo sat as if blandly unconscious of it all
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo does exactly what Amy asked and stays silent and cold on the first call.
paragraphs.simple: Amy looked relieved, but naughty Jo took her at her word. During the first call she sat with every part of her body calm and every fold of her dress right. She was as calm as a summer sea, as cool as a snowbank, and as silent as a sphinx. Mrs. Chester spoke of her 'charming novel', and the Misses Chester spoke of parties, picnics, the opera and fashions. Jo gave all of them just a smile, a bow, and a polite 'Yes' or 'No', in a cold way. Amy sent her the message 'Talk' and tried to draw her out, and even kicked her softly. Jo sat as if she did not know about any of it. Her manner was like Maud's face: 'icily regular, splendidly null'.

paragraphs.context: As she spoke, Amy returned her contribution, with a nod and a smile
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy gives May's things back with a friendly smile and leaves quickly, so that no one can thank her.
paragraphs.simple: As she spoke, Amy gave back May's things, with a nod and a smile. Then she hurried away, feeling it was easier to do a friendly act than to stay and be thanked for it.

paragraphs.context: “By and by I heard Fred’s voice, and then he came hurrying through the great arch to find me.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Fred hears bad news and leaves at once. Before going, he asks Amy not to forget him. Amy says nothing, but she looks at him.
paragraphs.simple: Later Amy heard Fred's voice, and he came hurrying through the great arch to find her. He looked so troubled that she forgot herself and asked what was wrong. He said he had just got a letter asking him to come home, because Frank was very ill. He would go at once on the night train and had only time to say goodbye. Amy was sorry for him, and sad for herself, but only for a minute. As he shook her hand, he said in a way she could not mistake, 'I shall soon come back; you won't forget me, Amy?' She did not promise, but she looked at him, and he seemed happy. There was no time for anything but messages and goodbyes, because he left in an hour, and they all miss him. Amy knows he wanted to speak, but she thinks he promised his father not to yet, because Fred is a rash boy and his father fears a foreign daughter-in-law. They will soon meet in Rome. Then, if she does not change her mind, she will say 'Yes, thank you,' when he says 'Will you, please?' She says all this is private, but she wants her mother to know what is going on. She asks her mother not to worry, because she is 'prudent Amy' and will do nothing rashly. She asks for advice, and says she will use it if she can. She wishes she could talk with Marmee and asks her mother to love and trust her.

paragraphs.context: Now, the old sofa was a regular patriarch of a sofa
paragraphs.mainIdea: The old family sofa has been used by the girls all their lives. Jo's hard round pillow is her tool to keep people away.
paragraphs.simple: The old sofa was a true grandfather of sofas: long, broad, well-stuffed and low. It was a little shabby, as it well might be. The girls had slept and sprawled on it as babies, fished over its back, ridden on its arms, and kept animal shows under it as children. As young women they had rested tired heads on it, dreamed dreams, and heard loving talk there. They all loved it as a family refuge, and one corner had always been Jo's favorite lounging place. Among the many pillows that decorated the old couch was one that was hard, round, covered with prickly horsehair, and had a knobby button at each end. This ugly pillow was Jo's own. She used it as a weapon of defence, as a barricade, or as a stern way to stop too much sleep.

paragraphs.context: I went in, and while we worked I looked about me, for it was ‘a den,’ to be sure.
paragraphs.mainIdea: In a letter to Beth, Jo tells how she mends the Professor's things in secret. He finds out and offers to teach her German.
paragraphs.simple: Jo writes a funny letter to Beth. She teaches the children, Tina, Franz and Emil, and she likes the boys. On Saturdays she and the Professor take them for walks. She has now begun to take lessons. One day Mrs. Kirke asked her to help put the Professor's room in order, because she could not find six new handkerchiefs. The room was a 'den', with books and papers everywhere, a broken meerschaum pipe, a bird with no tail and a box of white mice. They found three of the handkerchiefs. Mrs. Kirke said he was so good-natured that the boys rode over him, and that he forgot to give her his things to mend. Jo said she would mend them, because he was kind to her. She mended his socks, and hoped he would not know. But she also wanted to learn German, because she could hear his lessons through the open door. One day he caught her studying, and laughed quietly. He asked if she wanted to learn German. Jo said he was too busy and she was too stupid. He said he had seen what the kind ladies did for him, and that he would give her a lesson as thanks. After four lessons Jo cried over the grammar, and he threw the book on the floor and went out. He came back happy and said they would read fairy tales together instead. Jo read with all her might, and he read to her from the story of the Tin Soldier, and they both laughed. Now she reads pretty well. She wants to give him something at Christmas, and she asks her mother for ideas. She is glad that Laurie is happy and busy, has stopped smoking and lets his hair grow. She is not jealous, and she thinks Beth manages Laurie better than she did. She thanks Heaven that Beth is comfortable.

paragraphs.context: She took to writing sensation stories; for in those dark ages, even all-perfect America read rubbish.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo secretly writes sensation stories. She goes alone to the editor, dressed in her best, and feels uneasy in the messy, smoky office.
paragraphs.simple: Jo began to write sensation stories, because in those dark times even perfect America read rubbish. She told no one. She made up a 'thrilling tale' and boldly took it herself to Mr. Dashwood, the editor of the Weekly Volcano. She had never read Sartor Resartus, but she had a woman's feeling that clothes can have more power over many people than good character or good manners. So she put on her best clothes. She tried to tell herself that she was neither excited nor nervous, and bravely climbed two flights of dark, dirty stairs. She found a messy room, a cloud of cigar smoke and three men with their heels higher than their hats. None of them took off his hat for her. This welcome made her a little afraid, and she stopped at the door and spoke with much embarrassment.

paragraphs.context: Jo wrote no more sensational stories, deciding that the money did not pay for her share of the sensation
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo stops writing sensation stories. She then writes a story full of morals, but no one buys it.
paragraphs.simple: Jo wrote no more sensation stories. She decided that the money did not pay for her part of the sensation. Then she went to the other extreme, as people like her do. She read Mrs. Sherwood, Miss Edgeworth and Hannah More, and then wrote a tale that was more an essay or a sermon, it was so full of morals. She doubted it from the start, because her lively mind and girlish love of romance felt as uneasy in the new style as she would feel in the stiff and heavy clothes of the last century. She sent this teaching gem to several places, but no one bought it, and she began to agree with Mr. Dashwood that morals did not sell.

paragraphs.context: Laurie was a young lover, but he was in earnest, and meant to “have it out,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Laurie is serious, and he is ready to say everything to Jo, even though his voice shakes.
paragraphs.simple: Laurie was a young lover, but he was serious. He meant to 'have it out' even if he died trying. So he began to speak at once, as he always did when his feelings were strong, in a voice that sometimes went husky in spite of his manly effort to keep it steady.

paragraphs.context: Now, Laurie felt just then that his heart was entirely broken, and the world a howling wilderness
paragraphs.mainIdea: Laurie feels his heart is broken and the world empty. But Mr. Laurence cleverly says some words that give him a little hope.
paragraphs.simple: Laurie felt at that moment that his heart was completely broken and the world a howling wilderness. But the old gentleman cleverly put certain words into his last sentence, and at those words the broken heart gave an unexpected jump. A green oasis or two suddenly showed in the howling wilderness. He sighed, and then spoke in a voice with no spirit in it.

paragraphs.context: Simple, sincere people seldom speak much of their piety
paragraphs.mainIdea: Beth does not explain her faith, but it gives her courage to wait for death. She says she tries to be willing, and she holds on to Jo's love.
paragraphs.simple: Simple, honest people seldom talk much of their faith. It shows in what they do rather than what they say, and it has more power than speeches. Beth could not explain the faith that gave her courage and patience to give up life and wait for death in a cheerful way. Like a trusting child, she asked no questions. She left everything to God and nature, the Father and mother of us all, sure that only they could teach and strengthen heart and spirit for this life and the life to come. She did not scold Jo with holy speeches. She only loved her better for her strong love, and held more closely to the dear human love, from which our Father never means us to be taken away, but through which He draws us closer to Himself. She could not say 'I am glad to go', because life was very sweet to her. She could only sob out 'I try to be willing', while she held fast to Jo, as the first bitter wave of this great sorrow broke over them both.

paragraphs.context: A little gray-coated sand-bird came tripping over the beach
paragraphs.mainIdea: A small sand-bird comes close to Beth. It comforts her and reminds her that the world is still pleasant.
paragraphs.simple: A little sand-bird in a gray coat came tripping over the beach, 'peeping' softly to itself as if it enjoyed the sun and sea. It came quite close to Beth and looked at her with a friendly eye. Then it sat on a warm stone, cleaning its wet feathers, quite at home. Beth smiled and felt comforted, because the tiny thing seemed to offer its small friendship and to remind her that a pleasant world was still there to enjoy.

paragraphs.context: At three o’clock in the afternoon, all the fashionable world at Nice may be seen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Every afternoon the Promenade at Nice is full of people of many countries, and the sight is as bright as a carnival.
paragraphs.simple: At three o'clock in the afternoon, all the fashionable world at Nice can be seen on the Promenade des Anglais. It is a charming place. The wide walk, with palms, flowers and warm-country bushes, has the sea on one side and the grand drive on the other, lined with hotels and villas. Beyond lie orange orchards and the hills. Many nations are there, many languages are spoken, and many costumes are worn. On a sunny day the sight is as gay and bright as a carnival. Proud English, lively French, serious Germans, handsome Spaniards, ugly Russians, quiet Jews and free-and-easy Americans all drive, sit or stroll here. They chat about the news and criticise the latest famous person who has arrived. The carriages are as varied as the people and get as much notice, especially the low basket-barouches in which ladies drive themselves with a pair of dashing ponies. Gay nets keep their wide flounces from spilling over the tiny carriages, and little grooms ride on the perch behind.

paragraphs.context: While Laurie listlessly watched the procession of priests under their canopies
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy sees that Laurie has changed. He is handsomer but tired and sad, and she does not dare ask why.
paragraphs.simple: Laurie watched without interest as priests passed under their canopies, with nuns in white veils carrying lighted candles and a group in blue singing as they walked. Amy watched him and felt a new kind of shyness. He was changed, and she could not find the merry-faced boy she had left in the moody man beside her. She thought he was handsomer than ever and much better. But now that the glow of joy at meeting her was gone, he looked tired and without spirit. He was not sick or quite unhappy, but older and more serious than one or two years of easy life should have made him. She could not understand it and did not dare to ask. So she shook her head and touched up her ponies, as the procession wound away over the arches of the Paglioni bridge and went into the church.

paragraphs.context: In France the young girls have a dull time of it till they are married
paragraphs.mainIdea: In France girls have a dull life until they marry. In America, the writer says, young wives are put on the shelf after the wedding.
paragraphs.simple: In France young girls have a dull time until they are married, and then 'Long live liberty' becomes their motto. In America, as everyone knows, girls sign the declaration of independence early and enjoy their freedom with republican spirit. But young wives usually give up their power when the first heir comes, and go into a life almost as shut away as a French nunnery, though not as quiet. Whether they like it or not, they are as good as put on the shelf as soon as the wedding excitement is over. Most could say, as a very pretty woman did the other day, 'I am as handsome as ever, but no one notices me because I am married.'

paragraphs.context: The poor man was very uncomfortable, for the children had bereft him of his wife
paragraphs.mainIdea: John feels shut out from home, so after six months he starts to spend evenings at the Scotts'.
paragraphs.simple: The poor man was very uncomfortable, because the children had taken his wife from him. Home was only a nursery. The endless 'hushing' made him feel like a rough stranger whenever he went into the holy area of Babyland. He bore it patiently for six months. When nothing got better, he did what other fathers in his state do and tried to find a little comfort elsewhere. Scott had married and set up house not far away. John got into the habit of running over for an hour or two in the evening when his own parlor was empty and his own wife was singing lullabies that never seemed to end. Mrs. Scott was a lively, pretty girl with nothing to do but be pleasant, and she did it very well. Her parlor was always bright and nice, with the chessboard ready, the piano in tune, plenty of gay gossip and a nice little supper set out in a tempting way.

paragraphs.context: Valrosa well deserved its name, for, in that climate of perpetual summer
paragraphs.mainIdea: The villa Valrosa is covered with roses everywhere, in a place where it is always summer.
paragraphs.simple: Valrosa was rightly named, because in that land of never-ending summer, roses bloomed everywhere. They hung over the archway and pushed between the bars of the big gate to welcome people passing by. They lined the avenue that wound through lemon trees and feathery palms up to the villa on the hill. Every shady corner with seats for resting was full of flowers. Every cool grotto had its marble nymph smiling from a veil of flowers, and every fountain showed red, white or pale pink roses bending down to smile at their own beauty. Roses covered the walls of the house, hung from its edges, climbed the pillars and grew wild over the rail of the wide terrace. From there one could look down on the sunny Mediterranean and the white-walled city on its shore.

paragraphs.context: It was not nearly so well done, but there was a life and spirit in it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Amy's second sketch shows Laurie as he used to be, strong and brave while taming a horse. It is a strong contrast to the lazy picture.
paragraphs.simple: The second sketch was not nearly so well drawn, but it had so much life and spirit that it made up for many faults. It brought back the past so strongly that a sudden change came over the young man's face as he looked. It was only a rough sketch of Laurie taming a horse. His hat and coat were off, and every line of the active figure, the firm face and the commanding stand was full of energy and meaning. The handsome animal, just beaten, stood with its neck curved under the tight rein. One foot pawed the ground impatiently, and its ears were up as if listening for the voice that had mastered it. In the ruffled mane, the rider's windblown hair and straight stand, there was a feeling of sudden stopped movement, of strength, courage and young life. It was in sharp contrast with the lazy grace of the 'Dolce far niente' sketch.

paragraphs.context: Here, cherished like a household saint in its shrine, sat Beth, tranquil and busy as ever
paragraphs.mainIdea: Beth is loved like a saint at home and keeps busy making small gifts for the schoolchildren who pass her window.
paragraphs.simple: Here sat Beth, loved like a holy person of the house in her shrine. She was calm and busy as ever, because nothing could change her sweet, unselfish nature. Even while getting ready to leave life, she tried to make it happier for those who would stay behind. Her weak fingers were never idle. One of her pleasures was to make small things for the schoolchildren who passed by each day. She dropped a pair of mittens from her window for a pair of purple hands, a needle-book for a small girl with many dolls, and pen-wipers for young writers working through forests of pothooks. She also made scrapbooks for children who love pictures, and all kinds of nice things. The children who were unwilling to climb the ladder of learning found their way covered with flowers, and they came to see the kind giver as a sort of fairy godmother who sat above and showered down gifts that suited their tastes and needs. If Beth had wanted a reward, she found it in the bright little faces always turned up to her window, with nods and smiles, and in the funny little letters full of ink blots and thanks.

paragraphs.context: Seldom, except in books, do the dying utter memorable words
paragraphs.mainIdea: Beth dies quietly and simply, as most people do, in the early morning at home, with one look and one small sigh.
paragraphs.simple: Seldom, except in books, do dying people say words that are remembered, see visions, or die with holy faces. Those who have seen many souls go know that for most the end comes as naturally and simply as sleep. As Beth had hoped, the 'tide went out easily'. In the dark hour before dawn, on the breast where she had drawn her first breath, she quietly drew her last. She gave no farewell but one loving look and one little sigh.

paragraphs.context: Amy’s lecture did Laurie good, though, of course, he did not own it till long afterward
paragraphs.mainIdea: Laurie does not admit that Amy's lecture helped him. He goes back to his grandfather and behaves well but will not return to Nice yet.
paragraphs.simple: Amy's lecture did Laurie good, though he did not admit it until long afterward. Men seldom do. When women give advice, men do not follow it until they have told themselves it is just what they planned. Then they act on it. If it works, they give the 'weaker vessel' half the credit, and if it fails, they generously give her all of it. Laurie went back to his grandfather and was so dutiful for several weeks that the old gentleman said the air of Nice had improved him wonderfully and that he should try it again. The young man would have liked nothing better, but elephants could not have dragged him back after the scolding he had got. His pride forbade it, and whenever the longing grew strong he made his mind firm by repeating the words that had hurt him most.

paragraphs.context: He had rather imagined that the denouement would take place in the château garden by moonlight
paragraphs.mainIdea: Laurie imagined a moonlit proposal. In fact the matter is settled on the lake at noon in a few simple words.
paragraphs.simple: Laurie had rather imagined that the end would come in the château garden by moonlight, in a most graceful and proper way. It turned out the opposite, because the matter was settled on the lake at noon in a few plain words. They had been floating about all morning from gloomy St. Gingolf to sunny Montreux. The Alps of Savoy were on one side, Mont St. Bernard and the Dent du Midi on the other, pretty Vevay in the valley, and Lausanne on the hill beyond. The sky was cloudless blue overhead, and the lake was a bluer blue below, dotted with pretty boats like white-winged gulls.

paragraphs.context: Now, if she had been the heroine of a moral storybook, she ought at this period of her life
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer says Jo is not a perfect heroine but a real girl. She is learning to do her duty, but cheerfulness takes longer.
paragraphs.simple: If Jo had been the heroine of a book that teaches good behavior, she would at this time of her life have become quite holy. She would have left the world and gone about doing good in a plain bonnet with religious papers in her pocket. But Jo was not a heroine. She was only a struggling human girl like hundreds of others, and she acted out her nature, being sad, cross, tired or full of energy as her mood suggested. It is very good to say we will be good, but we cannot do it all at once. It takes a long pull, a strong pull and a pull all together before some of us even get our feet on the right road. Jo had got so far that she was learning to do her duty and to feel unhappy if she did not. But to do it cheerfully was another thing. She had often said she wanted to do something splendid, no matter how hard. Now she had her wish, because nothing could be more beautiful than to give her life to father and mother and try to make home as happy for them as they had made it for her. And if hard things were needed to make the effort more splendid, nothing could be harder for a restless girl with big plans than to give up her own hopes, plans and wishes, and live happily for others.

paragraphs.context: “There is truth in it, Jo, that’s the secret; humor and pathos make it alive
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo's father says her little story succeeded because it is true and written from her heart, with no thought of money or fame.
paragraphs.simple: Her father said there is truth in it, and that is the secret. Humor and pathos make it alive, and at last she had found her own style. She had written with no thought of fame or money and had put her heart into it. She had known the bitter, and now came the sweet. He asked her to do her best and to grow as happy in her success as they were.

paragraphs.context: Jo was alone in the twilight, lying on the old sofa, looking at the fire, and thinking.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo is alone at dusk on the eve of her birthday. She feels tired and old and thinks she has done little, though she is wrong.
paragraphs.simple: Jo was alone in the dusk, lying on the old sofa, looking at the fire and thinking. This was her favorite way to spend the evening hour. No one disturbed her.
