She lay on Beth's little red pillow, planning stories, dreaming, or thinking gently of the sister who never seemed far away. Her face looked tired, serious and rather sad. Tomorrow was her birthday, and she was thinking how fast the years go, how old she was getting and how little she had done. She was almost twenty-five, with nothing to show for it. Jo was wrong about that. There was much to show, and later she saw it and was thankful.

paragraphs.context: The pillow was gone, but there was a barricade, nevertheless
paragraphs.mainIdea: A barrier of time and change stands between Jo and Laurie, but it passes quickly as they talk.
paragraphs.simple: The pillow was gone, but there was a barricade all the same. It was a natural one, raised by time, absence and change of heart. Both felt it. For a minute they looked at one another as if this unseen wall cast a small shadow over them. It was gone soon, because Laurie spoke, trying in vain to look serious.

paragraphs.context: “We have our plans; we don’t mean to say much about them yet, because we are such very new brooms
paragraphs.mainIdea: Laurie says they are new brooms with plans of their own. He will work hard at business so that his grandfather is pleased and he stays steady.
paragraphs.simple: Laurie says they have plans but will not say much yet, because they are such very new brooms. They do not mean to be idle. He will go into business with so much effort that his grandfather will be delighted and see that Laurie is not spoilt. He needs something like that to keep him steady. He is tired of wasting time and means to work like a man.

paragraphs.context: I cannot feel that I have done my duty as humble historian of the March family
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer says Daisy and Demi, the twins, are so adored that they are almost spoilt, and praises how early they could do things.
paragraphs.simple: The writer says she has not done her duty as the humble historian of the March family unless she gives at least one chapter to its two most precious and important members. Daisy and Demi had reached the age when they could think for themselves. In this fast age, babies of three or four claim their rights, and they get them, which is more than many older people do. If ever there was a pair of twins in danger of being utterly spoilt by love, it was these chattering Brookes. Of course they were the most remarkable children ever born. They walked at eight months and talked well at twelve months. At two years they took their places at table and behaved so well that all who saw them were charmed. At three, Daisy asked for a 'needler' and really made a bag with four stitches in it. She also set up her own house in the sideboard and used a tiny cooking-stove so well that Hannah cried with pride. Demi learned his letters with his grandfather, who made a new way to teach the alphabet by forming the letters with his arms and legs, so that head and heels were both taught. The boy soon showed a gift for machines, which delighted his father and drove his mother mad. He tried to copy every machine he saw and kept the nursery in a mess with his 'sewin-sheen', a strange thing made of string, chairs, clothespins and spools, with wheels that went 'wound and wound'. He also hung a basket over the back of a big chair and tried in vain to pull up his trusting sister in it. Like a loving girl, she let her little head be bumped until she was rescued. Then the young inventor said angrily, 'Why, marmar, dat's my lellywaiter, and me's trying to pull her up.'

paragraphs.context: Demi, like a true Yankee, was of an inquiring turn, wanting to know everything
paragraphs.mainIdea: Demi always wants to know the reason for everything, and he is upset when he cannot get a good answer.
paragraphs.simple: Demi, like a true Yankee, liked to ask questions and wanted to know everything. He often got upset because he could not get answers that satisfied him to his endless 'What for?'

paragraphs.context: Mr. Bhaer could read several languages, but he had not learned to read women yet.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Bhaer is confused by Jo's changing moods. Her words and looks seem to go up and down, and he cannot tell what she feels.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Bhaer could read several languages, but he had not yet learned to read women. He thought he knew Jo quite well. So he was very surprised by the opposite signs in her voice, face and manner. She showed him them one after another that day, because she was in half a dozen different moods in half an hour. When she met him, she looked surprised, though he could not help thinking she had come for that very reason. When he offered his arm, she took it with a look that filled him with joy. But when he asked if she missed him, she gave a cold, formal answer, and he lost hope. When she heard his good luck, she almost clapped her hands, and he wondered if the joy was all for the boys. Then, hearing where he was going, she said 'So far away!' in a tone of despair that lifted him to a high point of hope. But a minute later she knocked him down again by speaking like a person who was only thinking of the matter in hand.

paragraphs.context: It was certainly proposing under difficulties, for, even if he had desired to do so
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Bhaer asks for Jo's love in the street, in mud, with both hands full. His joy shines in his face so much that rainbows seem to form in the drops on his beard.
paragraphs.simple: It was certainly a proposal made under difficulties. Even if he had wished to, Mr. Bhaer could not kneel because of the mud. He could not offer Jo his hand, except in a manner of speaking, because both were full. He could not show tender feeling in the open street, though it was close. So the only way he could show his joy was to look at her. His face was so glorious that there seemed to be little rainbows in the drops that sparkled on his beard. If he had not loved Jo very much, I do not think he could have done it then, because she looked far from lovely. Her skirts were in a sad state, her rubber boots were splashed to the ankle, and her bonnet was ruined. Luckily, Mr. Bhaer thought her the most beautiful woman alive. And she found him more 'Jove-like' than ever, although the brim of his hat was soft and wet from the small streams running from it onto his shoulders (because he held the umbrella all over Jo), and every finger of his gloves needed mending.

paragraphs.context: “Boys. I want to open a school for little lads
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo says that the crop she will grow at Plumfield is boys. She wants a happy, homelike school, with Fritz to teach them.
paragraphs.simple: Jo says 'Boys.' She wants to open a school for little boys. It will be a good, happy, homelike school, with her to take care of them and Fritz to teach them.

paragraphs.context: Yes; Jo was a very happy woman there, in spite of hard work, much anxiety
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo is very happy at Plumfield in spite of hard work and noise. She has two little boys of her own, who grow up well among the crowd of schoolboys.
paragraphs.simple: Yes, Jo was a very happy woman there, in spite of hard work, much worry and constant noise. She enjoyed it fully. She found the praise of her boys more satisfying than any praise from the world, because she now told stories only to her flock of eager believers and admirers. As the years went on, two little boys of her own came to make her happier. They were Rob, named for grandpa, and Teddy, a carefree baby who seemed to have his papa's sunny temper as well as his mother's lively spirit. How they grew up alive in that whirlpool of boys was a mystery to their grandma and aunts. But they did well, like dandelions in spring, and their rough nurses loved and served them well.

sentences.context: Round shoulders had Jo, big hands and feet, a flyaway look to her clothes
sentences.simple: Jo had round shoulders, big hands and feet, and clothes that looked loose and untidy.
sentences.grammar: The order is turned around: 'Round shoulders had Jo' means 'Jo had round shoulders'. The writer puts the thing first for style.

sentences.context: Being still too young to go often to the theatre
sentences.simple: The girls were still too young to go to the theatre often, and they were not rich enough to pay for private plays, so they used their wits.
sentences.grammar: 'Being still too young...' is a participle phrase. It gives the reason for what the girls did next.

sentences.context: Serves me right for trying to be fine
sentences.simple: It is what I deserve for trying to be fine.
sentences.grammar: 'Serves me right' is short for 'It serves me right'. In talk, people leave out 'It'.

sentences.context: Believing that they could not begin too early to cultivate energy
sentences.simple: The parents thought it was never too early for the girls to build up energy, hard work and independence, so they agreed.
sentences.grammar: 'Believing that...' is a participle phrase giving the parents' reason. 'Could not begin too early' means 'it is never too early to begin'.

sentences.context: The atmosphere of the whole house being summer-like, Laurie led the way
sentences.simple: Because the whole house felt warm like summer, Laurie led the way from room to room.
sentences.grammar: 'The atmosphere ... being summer-like' is an absolute phrase with its own subject. It gives the reason for what follows.

sentences.context: If the roof of the house had suddenly flown off, the old gentleman wouldn't have been more astonished
sentences.simple: The old gentleman would not have been more surprised if the roof of the house had suddenly flown away.
sentences.grammar: This is an 'if' sentence about something imaginary: 'If ... had flown ..., ... wouldn't have been ...'. It compares Mr. Laurence's surprise to something that did not happen.

sentences.context: pride goes before a fall, and the revengeful Snow turned the tables
sentences.simple: Being proud leads to a fall, and Snow, who wanted revenge, changed things against Amy with terrible success.
sentences.grammar: 'Pride goes before a fall' is an old saying: proud people soon fail. 'Turned the tables' is an idiom meaning changed the situation so the other person now loses.

sentences.context: Although the oldest, Jo had the least self-control
sentences.simple: Jo was the oldest girl, but she had the least control over herself.
sentences.grammar: 'Although the oldest' leaves out 'she was': it means 'Although she was the oldest'. 'The least' is the superlative of 'little'.

sentences.context: she stood, like the jackdaw in the fable, enjoying her borrowed plumes
sentences.simple: She stood there enjoying the fine things that belonged to someone else, like the bird in the old story.
sentences.grammar: 'Like the jackdaw in the fable' is a comparison with an old story. A jackdaw is a bird that put on other birds' feathers to look fine. 'Borrowed plumes' means fine things that are not truly yours.

sentences.context: Hannah used to say, “I’d know which each of them gardings belonged to
sentences.simple: Hannah used to say she would know which garden belonged to which girl.
sentences.grammar: Hannah speaks in dialect: 'gardings' for 'gardens' and 'ef I see 'em' for 'if I saw them'. 'Which each of them gardings belonged to' is an indirect question.

sentences.context: Hoping to impress the lesson more deeply, Mrs. March, who had a good deal of humor
sentences.simple: Mrs. March had a good sense of humor. She hoped the lesson would stay in the girls' minds, so she decided to end the test in a fitting way.
sentences.grammar: 'Hoping to impress...' is a participle phrase placed first. It tells why Mrs. March acted, and 'who had a good deal of humor' is an extra clause inside it.

sentences.context: Tents, lunch, and croquet utensils having been sent on beforehand
sentences.simple: The tents, the lunch and the croquet things had been sent ahead, so the party was soon in the boats.
sentences.grammar: 'Tents... having been sent on beforehand' is an absolute phrase in the past passive. It tells what was already done before the main action.

sentences.context: Though possessed of half a dozen hats, it took him some time to find one
sentences.simple: Although he owned six hats, it took him some time to find one.
sentences.grammar: 'Though possessed of...' leaves out 'he was': it means 'Though he was possessed of (owned) half a dozen hats'. 'It took him some time to find one' uses 'it took + person + time + to...'.

sentences.context: I've got the key to my castle in the air; but whether I can unlock the door remains to be seen
sentences.simple: I have the key to my dream castle, but we do not know yet if I can open the door.
sentences.grammar: 'Whether I can unlock the door' is a noun clause that is the subject of 'remains to be seen'. The sentence also uses a key as a picture of a way to reach a dream.

sentences.context: Because if you care much about riches, you will never go and marry a poor man
sentences.simple: If you care a lot about money, you will never marry a poor man.
sentences.grammar: This is a real 'if' sentence (first conditional): 'if' + present tense, then 'will never' for the result.

sentences.context: who would as soon have thought of cutting off her head as her pretty hair
sentences.simple: Amy would have been just as likely to think of cutting off her head as of cutting her pretty hair.
sentences.grammar: 'Would as soon ... as ...' compares two things that are equally unlikely. It means she would never think of cutting her hair.

sentences.context: Hannah wisely allowed them to relieve their feelings, and, when the shower showed signs of clearing up
sentences.simple: Hannah wisely let the girls cry, and when their crying was nearly over, she came to help them with a coffeepot.
sentences.grammar: 'The shower' is a picture word for the girls' tears, like a rain shower. 'Showed signs of clearing up' means it was ending.

sentences.context: the house seemed like a clock whose pendulum was gone a-visiting
sentences.simple: The house seemed like a clock whose swinging part had gone away to visit someone.
sentences.grammar: This is a simile with a relative clause: 'a clock whose pendulum was gone...'. 'Gone a-visiting' is a playful way to say the pendulum is missing, just as Beth is the one who keeps the house going.

sentences.context: Down went Jo's face into the wet handkerchief, and she cried despairingly
sentences.simple: Jo put her face into the wet handkerchief and cried without hope.
sentences.grammar: The order is turned around: 'Down went Jo's face' means 'Jo's face went down'. A short word of place goes first for a strong effect.

sentences.context: So she took Amy in hand, and taught her as she herself had been taught sixty years ago
sentences.simple: So she took charge of Amy and taught her in the way she herself had been taught sixty years before.
sentences.grammar: 'Take in hand' is a phrase meaning 'take charge of'. 'As she herself had been taught' is a past passive clause that compares how she taught Amy with how she had been taught.

sentences.context: for the sincere wish to be good is half the battle
sentences.simple: Truly wanting to be good is already half of the fight.
sentences.grammar: 'Half the battle' is an idiom: the hardest part is already done. The 'for' gives the reason for 'I think you will prosper'.

sentences.context: I wish wearing flatirons on our heads would keep us from growing up
sentences.simple: I wish that wearing heavy irons on our heads would stop us from growing up.
sentences.grammar: 'I wish ... would keep' wishes for something that is not true or possible. It uses 'would' after 'wish'.

sentences.context: She was quite right, for the mischief-loving lad no sooner suspected a mystery than he set himself
sentences.simple: She was right, because as soon as the mischievous boy thought there was a mystery, he began to try to find it out.
sentences.grammar: 'No sooner ... than ...' means 'as soon as'. The first action came and the second followed at once.

sentences.context: straws show which way the wind blows, and I've made several discoveries today
sentences.simple: Small signs show which way things are going, and I have found out several things today.
sentences.grammar: 'Straws show which way the wind blows' is a saying: small signs tell you what is going to happen. 'Which way the wind blows' is a noun clause, the object of 'show'.

sentences.context: I don't know whether the shearing sobered our black sheep
sentences.simple: I do not know if the cutting of her hair made our wild girl more serious.
sentences.grammar: 'Whether' starts a noun clause, the object of 'know'. 'Black sheep' is a picture word for a family member who is wild; 'shearing' joins the sheep picture to the cut hair.

sentences.context: If Aunt March had begged Meg to accept John Brooke, she would probably have declared
sentences.simple: If Aunt March had begged Meg to accept John Brooke, Meg would probably have said she could not think of it.
sentences.grammar: This is a past unreal 'if' sentence: 'If ... had begged, ... would have declared'. It says what would have happened, but did not.

sentences.context: In order that we may start afresh, and go to Meg's wedding with free minds
sentences.simple: So that we can begin again and go to Meg's wedding with clear minds, it is good to begin with a little talk about the Marches.
sentences.grammar: 'In order that we may...' shows purpose. 'May' is a formal word here, like 'so that we can'. 'It will be well to begin' means 'it is good to begin'.

sentences.context: for ridicule is often harder to bear than self-denial
sentences.simple: Being laughed at is often harder to bear than giving up something you like.
sentences.grammar: This is a short wise saying. It compares two things with 'harder ... than'. The word 'for' gives the reason why the young man hesitated.

sentences.context: if they had not objected to taking advice as much as they did salts and senna
sentences.simple: She would have made the lessons easier if her children had not disliked advice as much as they disliked medicine.
sentences.grammar: 'As much as they did salts and senna' means 'as much as they objected to salts and senna'. The verb is left out. Salts and senna were bad-tasting medicines.

sentences.context: It takes people a long time to learn the difference between talent and genius
sentences.simple: People need a long time to learn the difference between talent and genius.
sentences.grammar: 'It takes + people + time + to...' is a common pattern. The word 'It' stands for the whole job of learning.

sentences.context: Not a golden penny, exactly, but I doubt if half a million would have given more real happiness
sentences.simple: It was not exactly a gold coin. But I doubt that even half a million would have brought more true joy than the small sum she got.
sentences.grammar: 'I doubt if half a million would have given...' uses 'would have given' to talk about an unreal past. The idea is that even much more money could not do better.

sentences.context: he practised as he preached, having waited patiently thirty years for fruit of his own to ripen
sentences.simple: He did what he taught. He had waited patiently for thirty years for his own fruit to become ripe.
sentences.grammar: 'He practised as he preached' means he did what he told others to do. 'Having waited' shows an action that was finished before the main one. 'Fruit' is used as a picture for his own work.

sentences.context: John Brooke laughed then as he never dared to laugh afterward
sentences.simple: John laughed then in a way that he never dared to laugh again.
sentences.grammar: 'As he never dared to laugh afterward' is a comparison clause. It tells us how big this laugh was: John never laughed like that again.

sentences.context: for even turtledoves will peck when ruffled
sentences.simple: Even gentle doves will peck when they are upset.
sentences.grammar: 'For' gives a reason. 'When ruffled' is short for 'when they are ruffled'. It means that even loving people can become sharp.

sentences.context: If it was fair —that was in the bond; and I stand to the letter of my bond, Shylock.
sentences.simple: The promise was only for fair weather, and I keep exactly to the words of my promise, as Shylock did.
sentences.grammar: 'Bond' is an old word for a signed promise. Jo makes a joke about Shylock, a person in a play by Shakespeare, who kept strictly to the words of his deal.

sentences.context: It’s a greater not to be able to hide them.
sentences.simple: It is a bigger misfortune not to be able to hide those feelings.
sentences.grammar: 'A greater' stands for 'a greater misfortune'. The noun is left out because it was in the sentence before.

sentences.context: Because they are mean is no reason why I should be.
sentences.simple: The fact that they are unkind is no reason for me to be unkind.
sentences.grammar: The whole clause 'Because they are mean' is the subject of the sentence. 'Be' stands for 'be mean'. It is a little unusual to start a sentence this way.

sentences.context: feeling that virtue was not always its own reward
sentences.simple: She felt that being good did not always bring its own prize.
sentences.grammar: 'Virtue is its own reward' is a well-known saying. Here the writer says 'not always' to make a gentle joke about it.

sentences.context: Don’t laugh, Jo; gentlemen really are very necessary aboard ship
sentences.simple: Don't laugh, Jo. Men really are very useful on a ship.
sentences.grammar: 'Don't laugh, Jo' is a negative order spoken to Jo. The rest, 'gentlemen really are very necessary', gives Amy's joking reason.

sentences.context: One of us must marry well; Meg didn’t, Jo won’t, Beth can’t yet, so I shall
sentences.simple: One of us must marry a rich man. Meg did not, Jo will not, and Beth cannot yet, so I will.
sentences.grammar: Each short part leaves out 'marry well' after the helper word: 'didn't', 'won't', 'can't', 'shall'. The pattern is a list that shows how Amy reasons, ending with 'so'.

sentences.context: Anything more wheedlesome than that touching appeal was seldom heard
sentences.simple: It was seldom that anyone heard a more coaxing, touching request than that.
sentences.grammar: 'Anything more X than that' is a comparison. The sentence is a way to say that this was the most coaxing request one could hear. It is built with a passive verb: 'was ... heard'.

sentences.context: Not a very romantic story, but it interested me
sentences.simple: It is not a very romantic story, but I found it interesting.
sentences.grammar: The subject and verb 'It is' are left out at the start, as is common in letters and notes. 'But' shows a contrast.

sentences.context: We’ll take this” (editors never say I)
sentences.simple: We will take this. (The writer jokes that editors never say 'I'.)
sentences.grammar: The part in brackets is the writer's own comment. It is a present-tense remark about all editors: 'never say I' means they always say 'we'.

sentences.context: but, thanks to the life-preserver thrown her by a friend, she came up again, not much the worse for her ducking
sentences.simple: But a friend threw her a life-saver, and she came up again, not much harmed by her dip in the water.
sentences.grammar: This is a picture: Jo took 'a plunge' into a 'sea' of sensation stories. 'Thrown her' is short for 'thrown to her'. 'Not much the worse for' means 'not badly hurt by'.

sentences.context: Not if you are the gentleman I think you.
sentences.simple: You will not stay, if you are the kind of gentleman that I think you are.
sentences.grammar: 'Not' begins a short answer to Laurie's last words. 'The gentleman I think you' leaves out 'to be': 'the gentleman I think you to be'.

sentences.context: it takes much folly, sin, or misery to send a young man to a violent death
sentences.simple: It needs a great deal of foolishness, sin or sadness to drive a young man to a violent death.
sentences.grammar: 'It takes + noun + to + verb' is a pattern for what is needed to do something. Here 'It' stands for the whole idea, and 'much folly, sin, or misery' is the thing needed.

sentences.context: for often between ourselves and those nearest and dearest to us there exists a reserve which it is very hard to overcome
sentences.simple: Often there is a wall of silence between us and those we love most, and it is very hard to break it.
sentences.grammar: 'There exists a reserve' is a formal way to say 'there is a reserve'. 'Which it is very hard to overcome' describes 'reserve' and has 'it' as a stand-in for 'to overcome it'.

sentences.context: he turned and strained his eyes to see the island which a greater usurper than even Napoleon now made interesting in his sight
sentences.simple: He turned and strained his eyes to see the island. A greater taker of power than even Napoleon now made the island interesting to him.
sentences.grammar: 'Which a greater usurper than even Napoleon now made interesting' is a clause that tells more about 'island'. A usurper is a person who takes power that is not his. Here it is a joke: the 'usurper' seems to be Laurie's feeling for Jo. 'Greater ... than even Napoleon' is a comparison.

sentences.context: the shock she received can better be imagined than described
sentences.simple: It is easier to imagine her shock than to say how big it was.
sentences.grammar: 'Can better be imagined than described' is a fixed pattern. It uses the passive voice with 'better ... than' to say that words are not enough.

sentences.context: if John goes on so much longer I might as well be widowed
sentences.simple: If John goes on like this much longer, it would be the same as being a widow.
sentences.grammar: 'If John goes on ... I might as well be' mixes a real 'if' with 'might as well', which says that one thing is no different from the other. 'Widowed' means that a husband has died.

sentences.context: as if he felt that justice was tempered with mercy
sentences.simple: It was as if Demi felt that being fair can be softened by being kind.
sentences.grammar: 'As if' introduces something that only seems true. 'Tempered with' means 'made softer by'. The verb phrase is in the passive: 'justice was tempered'.

sentences.context: Stir away; it won’t hurt me and it may amuse you, as the big man said when his little wife beat him.
sentences.simple: Go ahead and stir me up. It won't hurt me, and it might amuse you, as the big man said when his small wife hit him.
sentences.grammar: 'Stir away' is an order that means 'go on stirring'. 'As the big man said ...' adds a joke with a short story. 'It' stands for the stirring.

sentences.context: It takes two flints to make a fire: you are as cool and soft as snow.
sentences.simple: You need two flints to make a fire. You are as cool and soft as snow.
sentences.grammar: The first part says 'It takes + noun + to + verb'. The second part uses 'as ... as' to compare Amy to snow, which cannot make fire.

sentences.context: Blurred and blotted, faulty and feeble, as the lines were, they brought a look of inexpressible comfort to Beth’s face
sentences.simple: Although the lines were smudged and blotted, with faults and weak places, they put a look of comfort too great for words on Beth's face.
sentences.grammar: 'Blurred and blotted ... as the lines were' is an 'although' clause in an older pattern: adjective + 'as' + subject + verb. Then 'they brought ...' gives the main idea.

sentences.context: With the wreck of her frail body, Beth’s soul grew strong
sentences.simple: As her weak body fell apart, Beth's soul grew strong.
sentences.grammar: 'With + noun' tells us what was happening at the same time. It shows two things going in opposite ways, and the writer sets them next to each other for effect.

sentences.context: So well that I wish we might always pull in the same boat.
sentences.simple: We row so well together that I wish we could always share one boat.
sentences.grammar: 'Pull in the same boat' is a pun: it means rowing in one boat and also living one life together. 'I wish we might' uses 'might' for something that one hopes for but cannot be sure of.

sentences.context: men seldom do, for when women are the advisers, the lords of creation don’t take the advice
sentences.simple: Men seldom admit it, because when women give advice, men do not take it.
sentences.grammar: 'The lords of creation' is a joke name for men. 'When women are the advisers' is a time clause. The 'for' joins a reason to the first idea.

sentences.context: It was easy to promise self-abnegation when self was wrapped up in another
sentences.simple: It was easy to promise to give up her own wishes when her whole life was wrapped up in another person.
sentences.grammar: 'Self-abnegation' and 'self' are used as abstract nouns. 'Wrapped up in another' means fully busy with someone else. The 'when' clause shows the time when the promise was easy.

sentences.context: Frost opens chestnut-burrs, ma’am, and it takes a good shake to bring them down.
sentences.simple: Cold weather opens chestnut cases, ma'am, and it takes a hard shake to make them fall.
sentences.grammar: Jo answers Meg's picture of a chestnut-burr with another picture. 'It takes a good shake to bring them down' uses 'it takes ... to' for the effort needed.

sentences.context: Jo was mistaken in that; there was a good deal to show, and by and by she saw, and was grateful for it.
sentences.simple: Jo was wrong about that. There was much to show, and later she saw it and was thankful.
sentences.grammar: The writer speaks to the reader with a comment in the past tense. 'Saw, and was grateful for it' has two verbs that share the same subject, 'she'.

sentences.context: Blest if she ain’t in silk from head to foot?
sentences.simple: Isn't she dressed in silk from her head to her feet?
sentences.grammar: Hannah speaks in dialect. 'Blest if she ain't' is a shortened old form of 'I'm blessed if she is not', and here it works as a lively question. 'Ain't' is a non-standard form of 'is not'.

sentences.context: Not being a dog in the manger, but the happiest fellow alive, I assure you I can dance at Jo’s wedding
sentences.simple: I am not selfish like a dog in the manger. I am the happiest man alive, and I promise you I can dance at Jo's wedding with a heart as light as my heels.
sentences.grammar: 'Not being ... but ...' gives a reason, a way of saying 'because I am not ... but ...'. A 'dog in the manger' is a person who will not let others have what he cannot use.

sentences.context: it takes a gentleman to do it
sentences.simple: Only a true gentleman can do it.
sentences.grammar: 'It takes + noun + to + verb' shows what is needed. Amy says it takes a gentleman, and the word 'it' means helping others in a delicate way.

sentences.context: for honesty is the best policy in love as in law
sentences.simple: Being honest is the best way in love, as it is in law.
sentences.grammar: 'Honesty is the best policy' is a well-known saying. The pattern 'as in' adds a second area where the same is true.

sentences.context: If the boy had replied like Alcibiades, “By the gods, Socrates, I cannot tell,” his grandfather would not have been surprised
sentences.simple: If Demi had answered like Alcibiades, 'By the gods, Socrates, I cannot tell', his grandfather would not have been surprised.
sentences.grammar: This is an unreal 'if' sentence about the past: 'if ... had replied ... would not have been'. It compares Demi to a student in an old Greek story.

sentences.context: being a woman as well as a lover, she felt that, though it was too late to save her heart, she might her bonnet
sentences.simple: Because she was a woman as well as a lover, she felt that it was too late to save her heart but she could still save her bonnet.
sentences.grammar: 'She might her bonnet' leaves out 'save': 'she might save her bonnet'. 'Though' adds a contrast between the heart, which was lost, and the bonnet, which might still be saved.

sentences.context: he would have been glad of his handkerchief, if he could have got at it
sentences.simple: The Professor found it so touching that he would have liked to have his handkerchief, if he could have reached it.
sentences.grammar: This is an unreal 'if' sentence about the past: 'would have been ... if he could have got'. 'Glad of' means 'happy to have'. 'Get at' means to reach.

sentences.context: Nothing could be more natural or proper than for my Professor to open a school, and for me to prefer to reside on my own estate.
sentences.simple: It is the most natural and right thing for my Professor to open a school and for me to like living on my own land.
sentences.grammar: 'Nothing could be more ... than for X to ... and for Y to ...' is a way to say 'it is the most ... thing'. The two 'for ... to' parts name two actions that Jo calls natural.

sentences.context: I hope there will be more wheat and fewer tares every year
sentences.simple: I hope there will be more wheat and fewer weeds each year.
sentences.grammar: 'More ... and fewer ...' compares two amounts. 'More wheat' and 'fewer tares' use a picture from a farm to talk about good and bad in a family.
